lessons.title: Component Communication
lessons.lessonGoal: Learn how to pass functions down as props so children can communicate changes back up to parents, and understand the 'lifting state up' pattern for sharing state between sibling components.

sections.title: The Problem: Props Only Flow One Direction
sections.content: Lesson 3 established that props flow one-way, parent to child, and that a child cannot directly modify the props it receives. This raises a natural question: if a button inside a child component needs to cause some change in its parent (or in a sibling component), how does that actually happen, given this one-way restriction? The answer is a specific, deliberate pattern: a parent passes a function down to its child as a prop, and the child calls that function (typically in response to an event) when it wants to communicate that something happened or request some change — the parent remains fully in control of how it actually responds to that function being called, including whether or how its own state changes as a result.

sections.title: A Doorbell, Not A Key To The House
sections.content: Think of a child component being handed a callback function from its parent like being handed a doorbell button rather than a house key. The child can press the doorbell (call the function) to notify the parent that something happened, but the child has no actual ability to walk in and rearrange the furniture itself (directly modify the parent's state) — only the parent, hearing the doorbell, decides exactly what to do in response, including whether to update its own internal state at all. This preserves the same one-way, predictable data flow established in lesson 3: the child can request or notify, but the parent retains full, exclusive control over its own actual data, which is precisely why this pattern (rather than allowing direct mutation) keeps a growing application's data flow understandable even as it spans many components.

sections.title: Passing Callback Functions As Props
Lifting State Up To Enable Sibling Communication
sections.content: A more complex, very common situation: two sibling components need to share or coordinate around the same piece of data, but siblings cannot pass props directly to each other at all (props only flow parent-to-child). The solution is a pattern called 'lifting state up': the shared state is moved out of either sibling and placed instead in their closest common parent, which then passes that state down to both siblings as props — one sibling typically receiving the current value (to display it) and the other receiving a callback function (to request a change to it), or both siblings receiving both, depending on what each actually needs to do. This works because the parent, sitting above both siblings in the component tree, can pass props down to each of them independently, effectively routing communication between two components that have no direct relationship with each other, exclusively through the one component that's actually above both of them.

sections.title: Two Sibling Components Coordinating Through A Shared Parent
sections.content: This example shows a search input (one sibling) and a results list (another sibling) that need to coordinate, with the actual search term state lifted up into their shared parent:
sections.explanation: SearchInput and ResultsList are true siblings — neither is the other's parent or child, and neither has any direct relationship with the other at all. They coordinate entirely through ProductSearchPage: SearchInput receives the current searchTerm to display, plus onSearchChange (which is literally just setSearchTerm, passed straight through) to report changes; ResultsList separately receives that same searchTerm to filter its own results. Neither sibling needs to know the other exists — each only needs to know what its own parent gives it, and the actual coordination between the two happens entirely because they share the same lifted-up piece of state in their common parent.

sections.title: Where Lifting State Up Is Used Throughout Real Applications
sections.content: Lifting state up is one of the most common architectural patterns in real React codebases: a filter sidebar and a results grid, a set of tabs and the content panel they control, a form's multiple steps that all need access to the same overall form data. As an application grows large enough that many distant components need access to the same shared state, purely lifting state up through many layers of parents can become unwieldy (a problem sometimes called 'prop drilling', passing a prop down through several layers of components that don't use it themselves, just to reach a deeply nested one that does) — which is exactly the motivation for more advanced state-sharing tools like React's Context API or external state management libraries, typically covered in a later, more advanced module, once the limitations of pure prop-passing genuinely start to bite in larger applications.

sections.title: Common Component Communication Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Trying to have a child component directly modify a prop value it received, instead of calling a passed-down callback function and letting the parent handle the actual update — a direct violation of the one-way data flow established back in lesson 3.

2. Duplicating the same piece of state independently in two sibling components instead of lifting it up into their shared parent, causing the two copies to drift out of sync with each other the moment one updates without the other knowing.

3. Passing a callback prop with a confusing or generic name (like doStuff or handler) instead of following the onSomething convention, making a component's purpose much harder to infer just from its props.

4. Lifting state up further than actually necessary — placing shared state in a very distant ancestor 'just in case', when a much closer common parent would suffice, unnecessarily forcing props to be passed down through several uninvolved intermediate components.

5. Forgetting that a callback prop is just a regular function reference (following the no-parentheses rule from lesson 6) when wiring it up inside the child component that receives it.

sections.title: Centralizing Shared State At The Right Level
sections.content: Deciding exactly where a given piece of state should live — which specific component should 'own' it — is one of the most consequential architectural decisions in a React application, and it directly echoes the 'single source of truth' principle from lesson 4: shared data should live in exactly one place, owned by the lowest common ancestor that actually needs it, with everything below that level receiving it via props rather than maintaining independent, parallel copies. Placing state too low (duplicated across siblings) risks data drifting out of sync; placing it too high (in a very distant ancestor 'just in case') creates unnecessary prop drilling through components that don't actually care about that data themselves. Developing the judgment to place state at precisely the right level — not too low, not too high — is one of the central skills 'React Thinking' (the next and final lesson) is built around.

sections.title: Tracing Data Flow Through The Component Tree
sections.content: When two components that should be coordinating appear out of sync, the React Developer Tools' Components panel again becomes the primary diagnostic tool: select each component involved and check whether they're actually receiving the props you expect from their shared parent, and trace upward through the tree to confirm the actual shared state genuinely lives in one single place, rather than being accidentally duplicated independently in two different components. If a callback passed down as a prop doesn't seem to be doing anything when called, confirming — by checking the parent's own code directly — that the function actually updates state (rather than, say, only logging something without ever calling a setter) is a common and easy first check before assuming the bug is somewhere more complex.

checkpoints.question: How does a child component communicate a change back up to its parent, given that props only flow one direction?
options: By directly modifying the prop value it received
By calling a callback function that the parent passed down to it as a prop
Children cannot communicate anything back to parents in React
By using global variables to bypass the prop system
checkpoints.explanation: Parents pass callback functions down as props; children call those functions to notify the parent of an event, while the parent retains full control over how its own state actually changes.

checkpoints.question: Two sibling components both need access to the same piece of data, and one needs to update it based on the other's display. What is the standard React pattern for this situation?
options: Pass props directly from one sibling to the other
Lift the shared state up into their closest common parent, which passes it down to both siblings as needed
Duplicate the state independently in both siblings
Siblings cannot share data in React under any circumstances
checkpoints.explanation: Since siblings can't pass props directly to each other, shared state is lifted into their common parent, which distributes it down to both as props.

checkpoints.question: What problem does duplicating the same state independently in two sibling components risk?
options: No problem; duplicated state always stays perfectly synchronized automatically
The two copies can drift out of sync, since updating one doesn't automatically update the other
React will throw a compilation error
This is actually the recommended pattern for sibling communication
checkpoints.explanation: Duplicated state in separate components has no automatic mechanism to stay in sync; lifting it to a shared parent (a single source of truth) avoids this risk entirely.

codingChallenge.title: Coordinate Two Sibling Components By Lifting State Up
codingChallenge.description: Build a ColorPicker (a sibling that lets the user choose a color via buttons) and a PreviewBox (a sibling that displays the currently selected color as a background), coordinated through a shared parent that lifts the selectedColor state up and passes it down appropriately to each.

selectedColor state must be lifted up into the shared parent (ColorPickerPage), not duplicated in either sibling
ColorPicker must receive a callback prop (onColorSelect) and call it with the chosen color, never modifying state directly

lessons.title: React Thinking
lessons.lessonGoal: Synthesize components, props, state, hooks, events, conditional rendering, lists, and component communication into a repeatable process for designing a new React feature from scratch.

sections.title: What 'Thinking In React' Means
sections.content: Thinking in React is the specific design process of looking at a desired feature or UI mockup and systematically deciding how to break it into components, what data each component needs, where that data should actually live (as state, as a prop, or calculated on the fly), and how data should flow and change over time — done deliberately, before writing implementation code, rather than discovered haphazardly through trial and error. This lesson is this module's version of the closing 'mindset' lesson that appeared in Module 1 ('Engineering Thinking Basics'), Module 3 ('Frontend Styling Thinking'), and Module 4 ('Problem Solving Thinking') — it doesn't introduce new React APIs, but instead organizes everything from lessons 1 through 9 into a deliberate, repeatable design process you can apply to any new React feature you'll ever build.

sections.title: An Architect's Blueprint Before The First Brick Is Laid
sections.content: Earlier modules established useful comparisons: an architect's blueprint (Module 1) for understanding how the web works generally, and the same blueprint metaphor (Module 4) for the DOM specifically. Thinking in React is exactly this same architectural discipline, applied to a specific UI design before any code is written at all: a skilled architect doesn't start laying bricks the moment they see a building's intended appearance — they first identify distinct rooms (components), decide what each room needs to function (props and state), and plan exactly how plumbing and electrical lines (data) should run between rooms that depend on each other, all on paper first. Skipping straight to writing JSX without this upfront design thinking is like starting construction without blueprints: technically possible for something small and simple, but increasingly costly and error-prone to course-correct as the building (or component tree) grows larger and more interconnected.

sections.title: The Five Recurring Tools From This Module
sections.content:
1. Component Boundaries (lesson 2) — break a UI mockup into a tree of components based on natural, single-responsibility boundaries, not arbitrarily.

2. Props Versus State (lessons 3-4) — for every piece of data a component needs, decide: does this come from a parent (props) and stay read-only here, or does this component itself own and change this data over time (state)?

3. Derived Versus Stored Data (lesson 4) — for anything that looks like it might need to be state, ask first whether it can instead be calculated directly from existing state/props during render, avoiding duplicated, driftable data.

4. Conditional And List Rendering (lessons 7-8) — identify which parts of the UI are genuinely optional, mutually exclusive, or repeated across a variable-length array, and apply the matching pattern (ternary, &&, early return, or .map() with proper keys) deliberately.

5. Data Flow And Ownership (lesson 9) — for any data multiple components need to share or coordinate around, identify the correct common ancestor to lift that state up into, rather than duplicating it or reaching for an overly distant ancestor unnecessarily.

sections.title: A Practical Five-Step Process For Designing A New Feature
sections.content: When given a new UI mockup or feature request, this module's tools combine into a concrete process: First, identify components — sketch the intended UI and draw boxes around each distinct, reusable piece, giving each a clear, specific name. Second, identify data — for the entire feature, list every distinct piece of information involved (a list of items, a currently selected filter, a loading flag, a form's current input value). Third, classify each piece of data — for each item from step two, decide if it's truly state (changes independently over time, owned by some specific component) or derivable from other data (calculated fresh during render, never its own state). Fourth, place state correctly — for each piece of actual state, identify the lowest common ancestor of every component that needs to read or modify it, and that's where it should live, passed down via props (and callback props, for components that need to request changes) to everything below. Fifth, identify rendering patterns — for each component, note where conditional rendering or list rendering with keys will be needed, and which specific pattern fits best.

sections.title: Applying The Five-Step Process To A Real Feature Request
sections.content: Request: 'Build a task list where users can filter by status (all/active/completed) and toggle individual tasks complete.' Here's how the five steps apply, before any implementation code is written:
sections.explanation: Every implementation decision in the final code traces directly back to one of the five planning steps completed before any JSX was written: the component boundaries match step 1 exactly, tasks and selectedFilter are state because step 3 classified them that way, filteredTasks is deliberately NOT its own state because step 3 also classified it as derivable, and both pieces of actual state live in TaskFilterPage specifically because step 4 identified it as the correct common ancestor. This is precisely the discipline 'thinking in React' refers to — the planning happened first, and the code that followed was almost mechanical once the plan was solid.

sections.title: How This Process Shows Up In Real React Engineering Work
sections.content: This exact five-step thinking process (or something very close to it) is how experienced React developers approach unfamiliar feature requests and code review alike: a reviewer noticing 'this should probably be derived instead of its own state' or 'this state should be lifted up to the parent both of these components share' is applying steps 3 and 4 directly, out loud, on a real pull request. Technical interviews for React-focused roles frequently present exactly this kind of 'design this component structure for the following mockup' question, evaluating precisely this planning skill rather than syntax memorization. As applications grow large enough that this manual process becomes genuinely difficult to apply by hand across dozens of interrelated components, more advanced state management tools (briefly mentioned in lesson 9, and explored in later, more advanced modules) become valuable — but they augment this same underlying thinking, rather than replacing the need for it.

sections.title: What Happens Without This Process
sections.content: Developers who skip this kind of upfront planning and start writing JSX immediately for any non-trivial feature often end up: storing derived data as its own separate state that drifts out of sync (skipping step 3), placing shared state too low (duplicated across siblings) or too high (over-broad prop drilling) because no one identified the correct common ancestor deliberately (skipping step 4), or building components with unclear, overlapping responsibilities because no one drew clean component boundaries before starting (skipping step 1). These issues are typically still fixable after the fact, but cost significantly more effort to untangle once a feature is already partially built around the wrong structure, compared to the relatively small upfront cost of working through this five-step process before writing any implementation code at all.

sections.title: Fundamentals Are Still The Real Curriculum
sections.content: This lesson is the fourth time this curriculum has explicitly named this theme (Module 1, Module 3, Module 4, and now Module 6): the specific tool or library changes, but the underlying decomposition discipline — identify the pieces, identify the data, classify that data correctly, place it at the right level of ownership, and choose rendering patterns deliberately — is what actually transfers from project to project, framework to framework, and year to year of your career. Everything you'll learn in upcoming modules (Next.js, more advanced state management, backend integration) will assume you can already think through a feature this way; React's specific hooks and JSX syntax are simply this module's particular vehicle for practicing a kind of structured thinking that long outlasts any single library's popularity.

sections.title: Auditing Your Own Component Designs
sections.content: A valuable habit, directly mirroring the self-audit techniques from this curriculum's previous closing lessons, is to revisit a React component you've already built and walk it back through these five steps in reverse: are this component's boundaries genuinely clean, single-responsibility ones, or did several unrelated concerns get tangled into one component? Is every piece of state genuinely independent information, or is some of it secretly derivable from other state/props you already have? Does every piece of state live at the lowest common ancestor that actually needs it, or has it drifted too high or too low over the course of development? Running this audit — including on the coding challenges from this very module — is one of the most effective ways to convert React syntax knowledge into the kind of deliberate architectural judgment this lesson, and 'thinking in React' generally, is named for.

checkpoints.question: According to this lesson's five-step process, what should you determine immediately after identifying a feature's components?
options: Which CSS framework to use for styling
Every distinct piece of data involved in the feature, before deciding where each piece should live
How many total lines of code the feature will require
Which third-party library to install first
checkpoints.explanation: Step 2 in the framework is identifying all the data involved, which is a necessary precursor to correctly classifying and placing that data in steps 3 and 4.

checkpoints.question: While planning a feature, you realize a value can be calculated directly from two existing pieces of state using .filter(). According to this lesson's framework, what should you do?
options: Always create a new, separate piece of state for it regardless
Classify it as derived data, calculated fresh during render, rather than storing it as its own separate state
Pass it down through five layers of components just in case
Convert both existing pieces of state into derived data instead
checkpoints.explanation: Step 3 of the framework specifically calls for classifying calculable values as derived data rather than duplicating them as independent state, avoiding sync issues.

checkpoints.question: What is the central argument of this lesson's 'Fundamentals Are Still The Real Curriculum' section?
options: React's specific hooks and JSX syntax are the most important, permanent skill to master
The underlying decomposition and data-placement thinking transfers across frameworks and years, while specific tools and syntax change over time
Thinking in React only applies to React and has no relevance to other frameworks
Planning before coding is unnecessary once you're experienced enough
checkpoints.explanation: The lesson argues that the structured thinking process (component boundaries, data classification, state placement) generalizes well beyond React specifically, echoing the same theme from this curriculum's other closing 'thinking' lessons.

finalModuleProject.title: Rebuild The To-Do App As A Properly Architected React Application

finalModuleProject.description: Rebuild the To-Do App from Module 5, lesson 9 using React instead of vanilla DOM manipulation. The app must support adding, completing, deleting, and filtering tasks (all/active/completed), broken into multiple well-named, single-responsibility components, with state placed at the correct common ancestor and no unnecessary duplicated or derived-but-stored data. Begin by documenting your answers to the 5-step React Thinking framework as comments before writing any component implementation.

requirements.requirement: Documented answers to all 5 React Thinking framework steps (components, data, classification, placement, rendering patterns) before any implementation code
At least 4 distinct, single-responsibility components (e.g. a container, an add-task form, a filter control, and a task list/item), each correctly named
Tasks stored as an array of objects in state using useState, owned by the correct common ancestor component, not duplicated across siblings
A derived (not separately stored) filtered task list, calculated from the tasks array and the currently selected filter during render
A controlled input (bound to state, with a matching onChange handler) for adding new tasks, with an onSubmit handler that calls event.preventDefault()

The task list rendered using .map() with a stable, unique key (such as a task id, not the array index)

Component boundaries are clean and single-responsibility, with props (including callback props) used correctly for communication
State is correctly classified and placed at the right common ancestor, with the filtered list properly derived rather than duplicated as state
